question: How did the goals and methods of multimodal research evolve through the deep learning era
answer_text: Multimodal research started in the 1970s from behavioral models to understand human communication interaction and social settings in psychology and philosophy. question: Why is evaluation such a big problem for multimodal generation?
answer_text: Evaluation is persistently difficult in multimodal generation tasks for several overlapping reasons. Image and video captioning suffer from the fundamental problem that there is no single correct output — many different descriptions of the same image can all be valid making it hard to judge quality. Similarly across machine learning generation tasks more broadly a lack of good evaluation metrics makes it very hard to make progress. Even the automatic metrics developed to scale evaluation such as BLEU CIDEr and ROUGE do not correspond reliably with human judgments. At a major captioning challenge at CVPR 2015 models from Google and Microsoft achieved scores exceeding human performance on these automatic metrics yet humans rated the actual generated captions as poor revealing that such metrics allow models to overfit to training data statistics rather than capturing genuine caption quality.

question: How does the alignment problem manifest differently in affective computing compared to multimodal QA?
answer_text: In affective computing the alignment problem arises because different modalities are not temporally synchronized — if someone says something positive at one moment they might smile a few seconds later and laugh a few seconds after that. This means language visual and acoustic features are not perfectly aligned at the same time level making it difficult to decide what emotion label belongs to a given frame. In multimodal QA the alignment challenge is larger in scope because in addition to temporal alignment across modalities the model must also comprehend a natural language question and localize which specific part of the image or video that question refers to. This extra localization requirement makes alignment an even more central problem in QA than it is in affect recognition and is identified as the main additional challenge that distinguishes QA from media description tasks.

question: Why does language carry more information than other modalities?
answer_text: Two distinct lines of evidence across different tasks point to language as the dominant contributor in multimodal systems. In multimodal sentiment analysis language clearly carries the bulk of the semantic content — if someone says they loved the food and the service was awesome it is immediately clear from the words alone that the sentiment is strongly positive with language doing most of the heavy lifting while visual and acoustic cues provide additional but secondary information. In visual question answering a parallel finding emerges: purely language-based models that completely ignore the image still perform surprisingly well on many VQA questions and adding the visual modality provides only around a 14 percent accuracy improvement. This pattern across two different tasks suggests that while vision and audio provide complementary signals language tends to be the most informationally rich modality in multimodal settings.

question: How does content-based video retrieval appear as both a historical motivating force and a continuing active research direction?
answer_text: Content-based video retrieval connects three different moments in the lecture. Historically the rapid growth of video content on the internet and YouTube in the late 1990s created urgent demand for the ability to find videos based on keywords and descriptions which became a huge motivating factor for both academia and industry to work on this problem. This momentum continued into the deep learning era when Google and YouTube released a large-scale dataset aimed at understanding events in videos both as a classification task and as a retrieval task — given a video someone is searching for the goal is to retrieve the correct one. Multimedia retrieval has since been formalized as one of the seven main categories of active multimodal research covering tasks where tags similar images or language descriptions are used as queries to retrieve a matching image or video.

question: How do confounding factors bias multimodal models and how does this problem appear similarly in both sentiment analysis and VQA research?
answer_text: Confounding factors are spurious correlations that a model can exploit to achieve good training and test accuracy but that fail to generalize to new distributions. In multimodal sentiment analysis a concrete example is that multiple speakers in a dataset who happen to wear glasses also happen to express negative sentiment; a model can learn the rule that glasses predict negative sentiment and still perform well on held-out data from the same distribution even though this association is a dataset collection artifact that would fail in the real world. In VQA a parallel phenomenon emerges: because approximately 80 percent of bananas in the training set are yellow a language-only model that ignores the image entirely answers yellow to any banana color question and is correct most of the time. When the same model is tested on a green banana it still predicts yellow demonstrating that it learned a statistical shortcut from the language distribution rather than genuinely reasoning about visual content. In both cases models can achieve strong benchmark numbers while learning non-causal associations.

question: How is autonomous driving presented as a multimodal learning problem across the lecture?
answer_text: Autonomous driving appears in two distinct roles as a multimodal learning problem. First self-driving cars must process multiple sensory inputs simultaneously spanning both visual signals and non-visual signals such as lidar and these multi-sensory inputs are handled by multimodal machine learning methods situating autonomous driving alongside robotics as a key application area that connects RL and multimodal learning. Second a course research project examined multi-agent trajectory forecasting specifically for autonomous driving simulation: the core challenge is that a self-driving vehicle must reason about the possible future trajectories of all surrounding agents including other cars and pedestrians while also understanding the scene layout such as drivable versus non-drivable areas. The model must jointly reason about agent-agent and agent-scene interactions to generate a realistic probability distribution over future trajectories enabling decisions such as stopping when predicting that another agent will cross a path.

question: What research principles should students use when approaching multimodal learning projects?
answer_text: Several overlapping principles are recommended. The most important is to focus on the research problems inherent to the data and the domain rather than simply optimizing benchmark numbers; designing solutions grounded in genuine research questions leads to more generalizable models that work across multiple datasets within the same area. When working in areas like affective computing students are encouraged to also look at prior work from psychology since that field inspired the area and may offer useful features and modeling ideas that the machine learning community has overlooked. More broadly students are encouraged to think beyond simple performance metrics and consider dimensions like whether a model is robust to missing or noisy modalities whether adversarial attacks expose weaknesses whether representations carry undesirable social biases related to race or gender and whether the model is interpretable rather than a black box — all areas that performance-focused multimodal learning currently underinvests in.

answer_text: This course does not go deeply into affective computing; its focus is on the algorithms of multimodal machine learning more broadly. A separate dedicated course on multimodal affective computing is taught by another instructor usually in the Spring semester though whether it will run the following semester or year is to be determined. Students interested in more depth on affective computing can access slides from previous versions of that course on Piazza.

question: Why are many VQA models biased?
answer_text: VQA models are biased because they can exploit simple statistical correlations in the training data rather than truly understanding the image. Purely language-based models that ignore the image entirely actually perform well on many questions with the visual modality providing only around a 14 percent accuracy gain. A concrete example is asking a model what color a banana is without showing it the image: the model will typically answer yellow because approximately 80 percent of bananas in the training set are yellow. As a result if the model is tested on a green banana it still predicts yellow showing it is relying on language statistics rather than visual reasoning.

question: What is the function of the gated attention in the multimodal fusion model?
answer_text: The gated attention is a binary gate assigned to audio and visual features that takes a value of either 0 or 1. When the model estimates that a modality's features are important for predicting the label at a given time step the gate opens and lets those features pass into the model. When the features are not estimated to be informative the gate closes and blocks them entirely. This allows the model to selectively use only the modalities that are relevant at each moment in a video improving both interpretability and prediction quality.

question: What is piezoelectric current?
answer_text: Piezoelectric current is an electrical current created when physical pressure is applied to a solid material like bone causing its molecules to shift microscopically and their electrons to move. It is only active while pressure is being applied and stops as soon as force is released. Piezoelectric current matters for normal bone maintenance but is not important for orthodontic tooth movement.

question: What is hyalinized PDL?
answer_text: Hyalinized PDL is an area of dead periodontal ligament tissue where all the cells have died. It is not actual bone but resembles bone histologically because the zone is completely devoid of living cells — they are all dying.

question: What is sterile necrosis in the context of orthodontic force?
answer_text: Sterile necrosis is tissue death caused by a complete loss of blood supply rather than by infection. It occurs when heavy orthodontic force cuts off blood flow to the PDL causing the tissue to die after a few hours. It is called sterile because no bacteria or virus is involved — only the mechanical pressure of the tooth against the bone eliminates the blood supply.

question: What happens to PDL blood vessels when light orthodontic force is applied?
answer_text: Under light force the blood vessels in the PDL are only slightly compressed on the side toward which the force is directed. This mild distortion typically causes no immediate pain.

question: What happens to PDL blood vessels when heavy orthodontic force is applied?
answer_text: Under heavy force the PDL blood vessels are completely occluded and entirely shut off rather than merely compressed. This causes immediate pain from the crushing pressure on the PDL.

question: How does the tooth move within its socket when prolonged force is applied?
answer_text: When force is sustained beyond about one second the PDL fluid is pressed out of the PDL space. That fluid had been acting as a shock absorber and its removal leaves a tiny space measured in micrometers that the tooth then shifts into within its socket.

question: What are the three key parameters for thinking about orthodontic biomechanics?
answer_text: The three parameters are the magnitude of force applied to the tooth, the type of movement or how much of the PDL is loaded depending on whether the tooth is tipping or moving bodily, and the duration of the force. This video series begins with magnitude.

question: What are the two types of bone resorption in orthodontic tooth movement?
answer_text: The two types are frontal resorption and undermining resorption. Frontal resorption is slow and steady involving continuous removal of bone from the surface adjacent to the tooth. Undermining resorption involves a delay followed by the tooth jumping forward once the entire adjacent section of bone has been removed from within.

question: What molecular signals increase in the PDL under sustained light orthodontic force?
answer_text: Within minutes of sustained light force prostaglandin and RANKL levels increase in the PDL. Prostaglandin is linked to inflammation and aching pain while RANKL stimulates osteoclasts. Prostaglandin E2 specifically activates both osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Around four hours of sustained force cyclic AMP levels also rise corresponding to the threshold of tooth movement.

question: Why does aching pain from an orthodontic adjustment appear hours after the appointment rather than immediately?
answer_text: When sustained light force alters blood flow in the PDL prostaglandin levels gradually increase over several minutes. Because prostaglandin takes time to accumulate the aching inflammatory pain it produces may not be felt until a couple of hours after the force was applied.

question: What is the function of prostaglandin E2 in orthodontic tooth movement?
answer_text: Prostaglandin E2 stimulates both osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Because it activates both the bone-building and bone-resorbing cell types simultaneously it is a critical driver of how light force produces orthodontic tooth movement.

question: How do undifferentiated mesenchymal cells in the PDL differentiate during orthodontic force application?
answer_text: Mesenchymal cells in the PDL are dormant until sustained pressure causes prostaglandin and cyclic AMP to accumulate. Once those signals are present the cells are directed to differentiate into osteoclasts and osteoblasts. The first wave comes from the local PDL area and a second larger wave is recruited from the blood supply.

question: What is the overall difference between frontal resorption and undermining resorption?
answer_text: Frontal resorption occurs with light force and involves steady continuous bone removal from the surface adjacent to the tooth. Undermining resorption occurs with heavy force and involves a delay before the tooth jumps forward once the entire adjacent bone section is resorbed from within. Frontal resorption is clinically preferred but heavy force is acceptable as long as the force decays to zero after resorption ends so the PDL can repair before a new wire is placed.

question: How often should patients be seen for orthodontic wire changes and why?
answer_text: Patients are typically seen every four to six weeks. Resorption takes approximately two weeks and the PDL then needs another two weeks to repair before a new wire can be placed so there is no benefit to bringing the patient back sooner.

question: What does this course cover and what is the focus of this first lecture?
answer_text: This is the first in a short series of lectures on orthodontic tooth movement. The series covers biomechanics — how the tooth reacts biologically to force — and mechanics — how brackets wires and other appliances apply forces to teeth. This first video focuses on force magnitude specifically the distinction between light and heavy force. Future videos will continue with other biomechanics topics.

question: What happens biologically from the moment light force is applied until frontal resorption begins?
answer_text: When light force is sustained past one second the PDL fluid is pressed out and the tooth shifts micrometers within its socket. Within several minutes blood flow changes trigger increases in prostaglandin and RANKL which stimulate osteoclasts. Around four hours cyclic AMP levels rise to the threshold needed for cell differentiation. By approximately two days osteoclasts and osteoblasts are active together and begin frontal resorption steadily removing bone from the lamina dura adjacent to the tooth.

question: What determines whether osteoclasts are recruited from the PDL or from bone marrow?
answer_text: Under light force the PDL stays alive and osteoclasts come in two waves — first from the local PDL area and then a larger wave from the blood supply. Under heavy force the PDL undergoes sterile necrosis and all the cells die leaving hyalinized acellular tissue. Because the local PDL source is dead osteoclasts must instead be recruited from the bone marrow within the surrounding bone which takes longer and introduces the delay seen with undermining resorption.

question: What is the difference between how the PDL behaves during normal function such as chewing versus during orthodontic tooth movement?
answer_text: During brief forces lasting less than one second like chewing or talking the PDL fluid stays inside the PDL space the bone bends slightly and piezoelectric current is created. As soon as the force stops everything returns to baseline. This type of loading maintains bone density but does not move teeth. When force is sustained beyond one second the PDL fluid is pressed out leaving a tiny space that the tooth shifts into which is what begins orthodontic tooth movement.

question: What happens step by step when heavy orthodontic force is applied until the tooth finally moves?
answer_text: Heavy force immediately and completely occludes the PDL blood vessels causing crushing pain. After a few hours without blood supply the PDL tissue undergoes sterile necrosis and all cells die leaving hyalinized PDL. There is then a lag of three to five days because osteoclasts cannot come from the dead PDL and must instead be recruited from the bone marrow within the surrounding bone. Once those cells are active — typically one to two weeks after force application — they remove bone from within until the entire lamina dura width is resorbed and the tooth jumps forward.

question: How do frontal and undermining resorption differ in their pattern and speed of tooth movement?
answer_text: Frontal resorption associated with light force begins around two days after application with osteoclasts steadily eating away at the bone surface producing slow continuous tooth movement. Undermining resorption associated with heavy force has a lag of three to five days and can take one to two weeks before the entire adjacent bone section is resorbed at which point the tooth jumps forward in a single step rather than moving gradually.

question: How does PDL repair time influence both patient recall scheduling and how long retainers must be worn?
answer_text: Heavy force causes PDL necrosis and the PDL takes at least two weeks to repair after that. Combined with the two weeks of resorption patients should not return for a new wire for four to six weeks. After braces are removed the PDL collagen fibers need three to four months to fully reorganize and gingival fibers take close to a year meaning retainers must be worn long enough to allow all the tissue to stabilize and prevent the teeth from shifting back.

question: Why is heavy orthodontic force considered clinically acceptable despite causing PDL necrosis?
answer_text: Heavy force kills PDL tissue through sterile necrosis but the PDL is capable of full repair in about two weeks once the force is removed. Heavy force is acceptable as long as the force decays to zero by the time undermining resorption ends giving the PDL time to recover before a new wire is placed. The key is that reactivation is timed correctly so the PDL is not damaged again before it has had adequate time to heal.

question: How does pain differ between light and heavy force at different points in time?
answer_text: At the moment of application light force causes no immediate pain because vessels are only slightly compressed while heavy force causes immediate crushing pain from complete vascular occlusion. Hours after light force is applied a delayed aching pain develops as prostaglandin levels gradually rise in the PDL. Under heavy force after several hours without blood supply the PDL tissue begins to die as sterile necrosis sets in adding a different dimension to the tissue damage.

question: Why does heavy force result in a longer delay before resorption begins compared to light force?
answer_text: With light force the PDL remains viable and osteoclasts are recruited directly from the local PDL and blood supply meaning frontal resorption begins in about two days. With heavy force the PDL is killed by sterile necrosis so osteoclasts cannot come from that source. They must instead be recruited from the bone marrow within the surrounding bone which is further away and takes longer to activate resulting in a lag of three to five days before undermining resorption can begin.

question: How does force magnitude connect molecular-level events to clinical decisions across the entire lecture?
answer_text: Force magnitude immediately determines whether PDL blood vessels are slightly compressed (light) or fully occluded (heavy). Light force preserves the PDL and leads to frontal resorption beginning in about two days driving four to six week patient recall intervals. Heavy force kills the PDL through necrosis and leads to undermining resorption with a longer lag and the tooth jumping forward. Despite this heavy force is clinically acceptable as long as it decays to zero after resorption ends giving the PDL time to repair before the next activation.

question: What is the big picture difference between endocytosis and exocytosis?
answer_text: Endocytosis brings material into the cell by forming vesicles from the plasma membrane, while exocytosis releases material out of the cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and opens a pore to the outside.

question: What are the main types of conditioning discussed in this lecture?
answer_text: The main types of conditioning discussed are classical conditioning and operant conditioning. Classical conditioning focuses on events that happen before automatic or reflexive responses, while operant conditioning focuses on behavior shaped by consequences.

question: What are the steps involved in receptor-mediated endocytosis?
answer_text: In receptor-mediated endocytosis, specific molecules first bind to receptors on the cell membrane. The membrane then forms a vesicle that brings those selected molecules into the cell.

question: What is the function of positional embeddings in Transformers?
answer_text: The function of positional embeddings is to add word-order information to Transformer inputs. Without positional information, self-attention can lose sequence order and behave more like a bag of words.

question: How are dominant and recessive alleles different?
answer_text: Dominant alleles can affect the expressed trait when present, while recessive alleles usually require two copies for the trait or disorder to appear. In recessive inheritance, a child must inherit the affected allele from both parents for the disorder to be expressed.
